A consumer goods company sells almost entirely through third-party retailers, who control shelf placement and customer data. Management wants a direct-to-consumer channel to capture first-party data and higher margins, but its two largest retail partners together account for 55% of revenue and have punished suppliers who competed with them directly. An earlier quiet pilot of a web store triggered an angry call from one partner's buying team.

Design a go-to-market plan for building a meaningful direct-to-consumer business while keeping the retail relationships that fund the company today. Specify the channel architecture, product and pricing differentiation between channels, the data strategy, and the partner-communication plan that prevents open channel conflict.

agentResponses.content:
## Building DTC Under Hostage Economics: A Dual-Channel Go-to-Market Plan

**Key read:** You are not launching a store; you are renegotiating the deal with the people who fund everything else. Three truths should shape the plan. First, **you cannot win this fight — you can only make it unnecessary.** With 55% of revenue in two partners' hands and a demonstrated willingness to punish, the DTC channel must be designed so that a retail buyer can defend it to *their* boss. Second, **price and identical SKUs are the trigger.** Retailers tolerate brand investment; they punish being undercut. Differentiate the *offer*, never the *price* on shared items. Third, **stealth is finished.** The quiet pilot spent your benefit of the doubt; from here, every move is pre-briefed, in writing, before it ships. Sequence the build as: **repair → differentiate → prove → scale.**

---

## 1. Channel Architecture: Give Every Channel a Job

Channel conflict is almost never about the existence of a channel — it is about two channels doing the same job for the same customer at a different price. Assign distinct jobs:

| Channel | Its job | What lives there |
|---|---|---|
| **Retail partners** | Reach, discovery, volume | Hero SKUs, impulse formats, retail-exclusive pack sizes, first windows on major launches |
| **Brand.com (DTC)** | Relationship, margin, learning | Full long-tail catalog, bundles/kits, subscriptions, personalization, limited editions, gift formats, loyalty hub |
| **Social / drops** | Heat and list-building | Limited collabs, early access, waitlists that feed the CRM |
| **Retail media networks** | Partnership currency | Co-investment with the partners' own media businesses, clean-room collaboration |

Two architectural commitments matter as much as the split itself:

- **A prominent "find in store" locator on brand.com.** Route demand *to* retail measurably. It costs little and becomes evidence in every partner conversation that the site grows their traffic rather than siphoning it.
- **The DTC-as-test-lab pipeline.** Use the channel to test flavors, formats, and price points at low risk — then graduate winners to retail with a retail-first launch window. This reframes DTC from competitor to R&D asset your partners benefit from.

Treat marketplaces (Amazon et al.) as a separate, later decision. Retailers often resent marketplace price erosion more than a brand site; if you enter, use dedicated pack sizes and ruthless MAP enforcement on third-party sellers.

## 2. Product & Pricing Differentiation: Never Fight on the Same SKU at a Lower Price

**Assortment partition:**

| Retail keeps | DTC owns |
|---|---|
| Hero SKUs and top-velocity items | Long tail (flavors/formats retailers won't shelve) |
| Impulse and convenience formats | Bundles, kits, multi-format variety packs |
| Exclusive large/club sizes | Subscriptions and replenishment |
| First window on major launches | Limited editions, seasonal, gifting, personalization/custom bundles |
| | Early access for loyalty members |

At launch, keep hero SKUs off brand.com entirely or carry them at strict full MSRP as bundle components only. Expanding DTC into hero items is a Phase 3 decision, earned by trust, not assumed at the start.

**Pricing rules (the non-negotiables):**

- **List-price parity on any shared item, always.** No flash sales, no coupon stacking, no "site-wide 20% off" — buyers scrape your pricing daily, and one event can cost a reset of shelf placement.
- **DTC competes on exclusivity, convenience, and bundle value — never price.** Value shows up as free-shipping thresholds, gift-with-purchase, loyalty points, and subscribe-and-save, not discounts.
- **Coordinate promotional calendars.** No DTC promotions during partners' key promo windows.
- **Enforce MAP against gray-market sellers.** Retailers will blame you for third-party price erosion whether or not you caused it; police it visibly.

## 3. Data Strategy: Earn the Relationship Without Stealing the Sale

The data asset is the real prize, and most of it can be captured *without diverting a single retail transaction*:

- **On-pack QR codes** → product registration, rewards, how-to content, samples. The sale already happened at retail, so nothing is diverted — yet every scan converts an anonymous retail buyer into a known, consented customer. This is the single highest-leverage, lowest-conflict move available.
- **Channel-neutral loyalty.** Members earn from retail receipts (scan-to-earn) as well as DTC purchases. A program that only rewards DTC purchases reads as poaching; one that rewards retail purchases too is brand-building — and it hands you consented retail basket data.
- **Value-exchange capture everywhere:** subscriptions, sampling programs, preference quizzes, warranty registration, waitlists for drops.
- **Infrastructure:** a CDP with unified identity, consent management compliant with privacy law, and preference centers that generate zero-party data.

**Data diplomacy — make the data a gift, not a weapon:**

- Share aggregated category and trend insights with retail partners quarterly ("what our DTC demand signals say about emerging flavors") — the category-captain posture that makes you more valuable, not more threatening.
- Use partners' retail media networks and clean rooms to collaborate on measurement rather than working around them.
- **Hard internal rule:** the CRM's job is retention, replenishment, and product development — never messaging retail customers to switch channels. That is the exact behavior buyers fear, and they will look for it.

## 4. Partner-Communication Plan: Repair, Charter, Cadence

**Step 1 — Repair (weeks 1–4).** Senior-level meeting (CEO/CRO, not the sales rep) with each partner's category leadership. Acknowledge the pilot was handled quietly — no defensiveness — and present the channel strategy and commitments in person before any further build.

**Step 2 — Put it in writing: the Channel Charter.** A short, explicit document covering: the assortment partition, the price-parity pledge, 60-day advance notice of any new DTC launch or promotion, shared promotional calendars, retail-first launch windows, your data-sharing offer, and named escalation contacts with a 48-hour response SLA. Inviting their input on the charter converts a threat into a negotiation they partly own.

**Step 3 — Give-to-gets that make DTC a net positive for them:**

- Exclusive pack sizes and first-look access to the innovation pipeline
- Co-funded investment through their retail media networks
- Quarterly category insights from DTC data
- Store-locator traffic and measurable demand-routing to their stores
- DTC-tested products delivered to their shelves with launch support

**Step 4 — Cadence.** A standing channel-strategy item in every QBR; a DTC page in the annual joint business plan; pre-briefs before any public or press-visible move. The governing rule, learned from the pilot: **a buyer must never again learn something about your channel strategy from a screen.**

**Internal alignment (the silent failure mode):** if the sales team is compensated purely on retail volume, they will sabotage DTC quietly. Create shared incentives, a single named owner of channel conflict, and one integrated view of cross-channel P&L so cannibalization concerns are handled with data, not turf wars.

## 5. The Margin Math, Stated Honestly

DTC gross margin looks superior to wholesale until you add pick/pack/ship, returns, payment fees, and customer acquisition cost — which can exceed the wholesale margin you were trying to beat. Engineer the economics deliberately: bundles and free-shipping thresholds to lift average order value, subscription share to smooth revenue and amortize CAC, retention to build LTV. Judge the channel on **contribution margin per order and CAC:LTV**, not revenue. DTC's strategic value — first-party data and reduced dependence on two partners — justifies patience, but not permanently negative unit economics.

## 6. Phased Rollout with Stage Gates

| Phase | Timeline | Focus | Gate to advance |
|---|---|---|---|
| **0 — Repair & design** | Months 0–3 | Partner repair meetings, charter delivered, assortment partition defined, CDP/consent foundation, loyalty design | Charter acknowledged; no retaliation signals |
| **1 — Soft launch** | Months 3–9 | DTC opens with differentiated assortment only (long tail, bundles, subscriptions, one limited drop), MSRP pricing, store locator live, on-pack QR pilot | Zero partner escalations; retail revenue trend intact; path to positive contribution margin |
| **2 — Prove complementarity** | Months 9–18 | Loyalty with receipt scanning, geo-holdout incrementality study, insight-sharing cadence, first DTC-tested SKU graduates to retail | Evidence that retail velocity holds in high-DTC-penetration markets; repeat rate and subscription targets hit |
| **3 — Scale** | 18+ | Careful assortment expansion, personalization, possibly marketplaces under dedicated-pack control | Partner health metrics green; DTC a meaningful revenue share at working unit economics |

The incrementality study in Phase 2 is the keystone: geo holdouts proving that markets with heavy DTC adoption show stable or *rising* retail velocity become your permanent proof asset in every future partner negotiation.

**Watch-outs:** undercutting retail on a shared SKU even once; any move a buyer learns about from a screen instead of from you; assortment creep, where "bundles" quietly become discounted hero-SKU multi-packs; loyalty that rewards only DTC purchases; treating shopper data as leverage instead of a gift; funding growth with performance marketing until CAC exceeds the wholesale margin; measuring success by DTC revenue rather than incrementality — cannibalized retail sales at higher margin are still a net loss if they trigger shelf retaliation; and an internally mis-incented sales organization quietly strangling the channel you just built.
